# Why the woman in the darker sleeves and dark apron takes things from the other workers

## Short answer

She is not one of the machine operators — she is the section's **collector / carrier**.
She takes the objects (the finished, wound coils) **from the operators so that the
completed work can be cleared away and passed on to the next stage of manufacture,
while the winders stay at their machines and keep working.** In other words, she is
doing materials handling: gathering up each woman's finished piece and stacking /
carrying it to the cloth-draped bench at the end of the row, rather than having
forty winders each stop and walk their own work down the aisle.

## What the film is

The clip is a Library of Congress paper-print copy (the leader reads "L.O.C.
FH45401" and the next frames show the 1904 copyright deposit stamp, "Copies
Received … 1904 … No. 45401"). It is one of the American Mutoscope & Biograph
"Westinghouse Works" actualities shot by G. W. Bitzer in the spring of 1904 — the
coil-winding room of the Westinghouse Electric & Manufacturing plant. It is a
single, continuous, slowly panning take with no titles and no sound, so everything
below is read off the action itself.

## What the room is doing

* Running away from the camera is a long double row of **coil-winding machines**,
  each with a large spoked hand-wheel and a circular/oval former. Each machine is
  worked by one woman, mostly in white shirtwaists.
* Down the middle of the aisle is a row of **very large spools/drums on stands**.
  Thin taut wires can be seen running diagonally from these spools up to the
  machines on both sides — the operators draw their wire from the big spools behind
  them and wind it onto the formers.
* At the near end of each row is a **bench covered with a light cloth**, with
  finished work lying on it (in close-up, parallel bar-like pieces are visible on
  the bench top) and loose tape/wire ends hanging over the front edge.
* A **male supervisor in a dark waistcoat and white shirt** walks slowly down the
  aisle between roughly 0:60 and 0:95, looking at the machines as he passes, and
  walks back toward the camera from about 1:40. He inspects; he does not carry
  anything. He is clearly a different person from the woman in question.

## Who she is and what she does

The woman in question is distinguishable from the operators because her bodice and
sleeves photograph distinctly darker/greyer than the bright white shirtwaists around
her, she has a white collar, and she wears an apron over the front of her dress.
She is clearest between about 0:11 and 0:20, standing in the aisle on the near side
of the spool row.

The behavioural facts that identify her role:

1. **She has no machine of her own.** Every other woman in shot is planted at one
   winding machine, with both hands occupied by the wheel and the wire. She stands
   in the open aisle, between the spool row and the end bench, with nothing in front
   of her to operate.
2. **She moves along the line rather than staying at one spot.** Over successive
   seconds she shifts position along the aisle and turns to face first one worker,
   then another.
3. **She repeatedly reaches across to the operators and closes her hands on
   something they hold out**, then straightens up, turns, and brings her hands down
   over the draped bench beside her — i.e. a receive-and-deposit cycle, repeated,
   with different workers.
4. **The direction of transfer is consistently away from the machines**: pieces go
   from the operators' hands to hers, and from her hands to the bench. She does not
   hand them back.

## The reason

Put those facts together and the reason is a straightforward **division of labour
aimed at keeping the winding machines running continuously**:

* A wound coil has to come off the machine and go somewhere before the next one can
  be started. If each winder carried her own finished coil to the end of the row,
  her machine would stand idle for the length of the walk, several times an hour,
  forty machines over.
* So one worker — this one — is assigned to go along the row, take each finished
  coil out of the operator's hands the moment it is done, and put it on the
  collecting bench (from which the coils go on to the next operation, taping and
  insulating, which the Westinghouse films show being done at separate tables).
* Her clothing fits the role: an apron and a plainer, darker dress are what you wear
  for fetching and carrying dirty, oily, wire-covered work, not for standing at one
  bench. The operators' good white shirtwaists are the giveaway that they are the
  ones who stay put.

So she is not taking the work away from them in any adversarial sense, and she is
not a supervisor confiscating it — the supervisor is the man in the waistcoat and he
does something visibly different. She is the runner whose whole job is to relieve
the winders of their completed coils so production down the line never stops.

## Confidence and alternatives

The core claim — that she is collecting completed work from the operators for
onward handling rather than doing any winding herself — is well supported by the
footage: she has no machine, she moves along the row, the transfer is always
machine-to-her-to-bench, and she never gives anything back.

Two related readings are possible but less well supported by what is visible:

* **Inspection / quality check.** She could be taking each coil to look it over
  before it goes on. This is plausible in principle, but an inspector normally hands
  the piece back or sets it in a reject place, and no return handoff is visible;
  also the actual walking inspector in this film is the man in the waistcoat.
* **Counting / tallying for piece-rates.** Collecting each woman's output would also
  serve to count it, which mattered in a piece-work shop. This is likely a by-product
  of the same trip rather than the reason for it — nothing in the frame shows her
  writing or marking a tally.

Note also that the print flickers heavily (early Biograph footage lit by Cooper
Hewitt mercury lamps), so individual garments brighten and darken frame to frame;
the identification above relies on her tone being *consistently* darker than the
white shirtwaists across many consecutive frames at 10 fps, not on any single frame.

## What the video shows (evidence)

1. **The setting.** The footage is an early 1900s factory floor (the leader is marked "L.O.C. #H45401", the Library of Congress copy of the 1904 Westinghouse Works film usually catalogued as "Coil winding machines"). Two long rows of women stand at identical winding machines, each with a large wheel. Down the aisle between the rows runs a long horizontal shaft of big spools/drums, and thin lines (the wire being drawn off) run from those spools to the machines. Stacks of pale, fringed bundles sit on the benches by the front machines – these are the wound pieces waiting to be taken away. So this is a room where many operators each produce small finished pieces at their own station.

2. **Who she is.** At about 0:49–0:51 (video time) a woman appears in the aisle next to the front-right machine. Unlike the operators, who wear white blouses, she has a grey/darker-sleeved blouse and a dark bib apron over a lighter skirt. She is not attached to any machine: she does not operate a wheel or handle wire; she stands in the walkway with one hand resting on the spool shaft, facing the operators.

3. **What she does.** She turns to the operator at the front-right machine, who has just finished a piece at her machine, and the two women bring their hands together at waist height: the operator hands over a small object and the woman in the dark apron receives it in both hands. She then immediately turns and moves on past the operator, carrying the item with her out of the frame on the right. She does not stop to use it, put it into the machine, or return it; she simply carries it off. That is the behaviour of someone gathering things from the workers, not of someone borrowing a tool or inspecting a machine.

4. **Why that means "collecting finished work".** The operators' job is to wind coils from the wire on the spools; each operator produces a stream of small finished pieces. Someone has to remove those pieces from the stations and take them to the next department. The film shows exactly that division of labour in the aisle: a man in a dark vest walks up and down checking the work (the supervisor); a boy in a vest and several other women come and go in the aisle bringing material to and taking things from the machines; and this woman in the dark apron goes from station to station receiving what the operators hand her and carrying it away. The woman with the darker sleeves and dark apron takes the objects because it is her job to collect the finished work (the wound coils) from the machine operators and carry it away from the work stations to the next stage of production, rather than because she is an operator herself or is supervising them. This is shown by her not being stationed at any machine, by her receiving a completed item directly from an operator's hands, and by her carrying it off out of the frame instead of using it or handing it back.

The room is a winding room. The row of workers on the left, mostly women in light blouses, each tend a small hand-crank winding machine. The long wooden drums down the centre are the bulk supply — wire, thread or insulating material — with strands running from them to the machines. What each operator produces is a small removable package wound in her own machine: a bobbin or coil. The cloth-covered table in the right foreground is a staging surface where rows of those small light-coloured packages stand in lines.

That is why the darker-dressed woman moves differently from everyone else. She is identifiable by her long skirt, darker upper clothing with darker sleeves, and dark apron, unlike the operators in light blouses, the boy in cap, vest and trousers, and the foreman in vest and tie. The operators stay at one machine and crank. She walks the aisle beside the supply drums, stops at one worker after another, takes a small object from the worker or from the machine, and carries it to the table. The clearest instance is around 48–51 seconds: she stands on the right of the drums, reaches her arm across the drums toward the left row where the boy with a tray is standing, takes the small object, turns toward the camera-right table, and bends over the table where the rows of packages are. Her behaviour shows routine clearing, not inspection, discipline or tidying:

- She takes from several different workers in succession, and each worker goes straight on working. There is no stoppage, argument or examination.
- She does not hold the object up, measure it, or hand the same object back, as an inspector would. She transports it away.
- What accumulates on the table is a growing set of uniform small packages, not tools, waste or personal items. That is finished product staged for counting, inspection elsewhere, or the next manufacturing step.
- The large supply drums cannot be carried by hand; only the small wound bobbins can be taken in one hand, which is what she is seen lifting and carrying.
